passage: "Vishal, can you dry the dishes?" asked his sister Rajni, not looking up from the sink. "Fiiiine," said Vishal, dragging the word out like a stretched rubber band. He took the towel and slouched over. Rajni stopped and turned. The word had said one thing and the length of it another. Was it sarcasm, or was he tired? He'd been up past midnight studying. "Is that a fine-fine or a fiiine?" she asked with a small grin. Vishal groaned, then laughed. "A bit of both. I'm tired, but I will do it." She handed him a plate. "Then I'll wash faster."

qa.q: What did Rajni ask Vishal to do?
qa.a: She asked him to dry the dishes.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when he dragged out the word "fiiine"?
qa.a: He was probably tired and a little reluctant, though he agreed to help. He confirmed it was a bit of both.

qa.q: What worked in the way Rajni responded?
qa.a: She noticed the mismatch between the word and its length, then asked lightly which kind of fine it was. That let him say what he felt.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Rajni's teasing question?
qa.a: He may feel understood rather than told off, since he laughed and admitted the truth. A sharper reply might have made him defensive.

grounding: A teenager drags out the word fine, signalling reluctance or tiredness, and a sibling reads both the word and rhythm and asks.

passage:
"Lakshmi, phone off, please. Dinner."
"Fiiiine."
"That sounded like sarcasm."
"It was, a bit. I was in the middle of a video." Lakshmi put the phone face-down. "And I'm annoyed because I know I've been on it too long."
"So it wasn't only about me?"
"No." She smiled a little. "It was half you, half me."
Bidisha laughed. "I'll take half. Come and eat."
"Fiiine," said Lakshmi again, and this time she was grinning. "That one was a joke."
"I could tell," said Bidisha. "That one had a smile in it."

qa.q: What did Bidisha ask Lakshmi to turn off?
qa.a: Bidisha asked Lakshmi to turn the phone off for dinner.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling behind her first "Fiiiine"?
qa.a: She was annoyed at being interrupted, and also annoyed with herself for being on the phone too long. Her admission that it was half Bidisha and half herself shows the mix.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do when the tone doesn't match the words?
qa.a: Bidisha can note the tone and ask lightly what's behind it. Reading both the word and rhythm avoids assuming.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi see Bidisha's remark about sarcasm?
qa.a: She might feel caught out but not attacked, since she answered honestly. The second fine came with a smile.

grounding: A teenager's drawn-out fine signals reluctance or sarcasm, and the other person reads both and checks.

passage: You asked how I got calmer in quizzes, Naveen? My speech used to race. In the quiz round I'd say the whole answer in one breath, like a train with no brakes, and then blank at the end. I'm Farhan, and my nerves were so loud I couldn't hear myself. You told me, "You sound like a train." I laughed, but it helped. So I practised: breathe out first, then speak, then stop at every full stop. Just stop. It felt slow, almost silly. But halfway through the next quiz my hands weren't shaking. The steadier pace made me feel calmer, not just sound it.

qa.q: What did Naveen say Farhan sounded like?
qa.a: Naveen said Farhan sounded like a train.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when the speech raced in quizzes?
qa.a: Farhan was nervous, and the nerves were so loud that Farhan couldn't hear the words. Racing speech was part of that anxiety.

qa.q: What could Farhan do before answering a quiz question?
qa.a: Breathe out first, then speak, and stop at every full stop. A steadier pace helps Farhan feel calmer as well as sound calmer.

qa.q: How might Naveen's train comment have felt to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan laughed, so it landed lightly, and it helped Farhan see how the speech sounded. It was said as a friend.

grounding: A teenager whose speech races when anxious practises a measured pace, and it helps the teenager feel calmer.

passage: Sonali had to read the morning announcements, and I stood at the side of the hall. She started so fast that the words ran together. Her hands gripped the paper. Then she stopped at a full stop, breathed out audibly and started again more slowly. Her shoulders came down a little. By the third sentence the whole hall could hear her. I can't know what she felt inside. Maybe she was nervous, maybe just wanting to finish. But her pace changed, and afterwards she said, "That was better when I stopped." I'm Mehak, and I told her it sounded steady.

qa.q: Where did Mehak stand while Sonali read announcements?
qa.a: Mehak stood at the side of the hall.

qa.q: What was Sonali probably feeling when she began so fast, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was probably nervous, since her hands gripped the paper and the words ran together. Mehak admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What could Sonali do again before her next announcement?
qa.a: Stop at each full stop and breathe out before starting. The slower pace helps her sound and feel calmer.

qa.q: How might the hall have heard Sonali's change of pace?
qa.a: They could hear her clearly by the third sentence, which likely made her sound more confident. It may also have helped her relax.

grounding: A teenager whose speech races when anxious pauses at full stops and breathes out, and a classmate observes the steadier pace.

passage: The storm knocked the power out just as Kiran sent her message: "Are you coming to study tomorrow?" She waited an hour, then two, staring at the dark screen. Nothing from Salma. Her mind started building stories. She's fed up with me. She found a better group. Kiran couldn't sleep, and the maths exam was at nine. At midnight she caught herself. She typed instead, "Hey, no pressure, but I'm worried I upset you. Are you okay?" She didn't expect an answer. In the morning it came: "So sorry! My phone died in the storm. See you at the library. Love you 😊"

qa.q: What knocked the power out?
qa.a: The storm knocked the power out.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while she waited for Salma's reply?
qa.a: She was anxious and worried she had upset Salma, and her imagination made up stories. The delay was actually because of a dead phone.

qa.q: What worked when Kiran finally asked?
qa.a: She sent a kind, direct message asking if Salma was okay instead of spiralling. Asking got a clear answer.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt when she saw Kiran's message?
qa.a: She felt sorry and warm toward Kiran, as her reply shows. She had no idea her silence caused worry.

grounding: A teenager waits hours for a reply and imagines rejection, then asks directly and learns the delay was harmless.

passage: Harish had asked Ojas at ten if he'd join the cricket group. By four, no reply. Harish checked his phone over and over on the way home. He'd seen "read" and nothing else. Does he think I'm annoying? he wondered. He'd had a hard day and his mind ran on. In the flat lift he stopped himself and wrote, "No rush, but are you busy? Just checking you got that." Ten minutes later: "Sorry!! I've been helping mum at her shop all day. Yes! I'll be there. Thanks for asking." Harish laughed at his own worry and pocketed the phone.

qa.q: What did Harish ask Ojas at ten?
qa.a: He asked if Ojas would join the cricket group.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he checked his phone?
qa.a: He was anxious and worried that Ojas thought he was annoying. He had also had a hard day, which fed the worry.

qa.q: What could Harish do next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: Wait a bit, then send a friendly message asking if the person is busy. That is wiser than spiralling.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt when he saw Harish's check-in?
qa.a: He was probably apologetic and pleased to be included. He had simply been busy with his mother.

grounding: A teenager waits hours for a reply, imagines rejection, then asks directly and finds the person was busy.

passage:
Nitin: so how did the audition go
Varun: it was fine, I just
Varun: ...
Nitin: you stopped mid-sentence
Nitin: want to finish?
Varun: not really
Nitin: ok. I'm here whenever
Varun: thanks
Varun: honestly I don't know if I'm sad or annoyed or just thinking
Nitin: that's allowed. no rush
Varun: the judges laughed at one bit and I don't know if it was a good laugh
Nitin: ah. that would bug me too
Varun: yeah
Nitin: cricket later? or just chai?
Varun: chai 🙂
Nitin: my treat. I'll wait at the gate
Varun: ok, give me a bit to pack up

qa.q: What did Nitin ask Varun about at the start?
qa.a: Nitin asked how the audition went.

qa.q: What might Varun be feeling when Nitin stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: Varun may be hurt, unsure or just thinking. Varun says it is unclear whether it is sadness, annoyance or thinking, and the judges' laugh bothers Varun.

qa.q: What worked in Nitin's reply?
qa.a: Nitin noticed the stop, gave space and said Nitin was around whenever. That left the door open without pushing.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt when Varun went quiet?
qa.a: Nitin may have felt concerned but chose not to press. Nitin offered options at the end.

grounding: A teenager falls silent or stops mid-sentence, which may mean hurt or thinking, and a friend gives space.

passage: At the well in the village, Ayesha was telling Kavitha about her brother's wedding when Kavitha laughed and said, "He must be the one who forgot the ring last time!" Ayesha stopped mid-word. Her mouth stayed open, then closed. She looked into the bucket. Kavitha wasn't sure. Was Ayesha embarrassed, hurt, or just thinking about the next part? She lowered her voice. "Should I not have said that?" Ayesha shrugged. Kavitha picked up one pot and said, "I'll walk you home. Tell me when you like, or not." They walked in silence, and at the gate Ayesha said, "It's just a sore subject."

qa.q: Where was Ayesha telling Kavitha about the wedding?
qa.a: She was at the well in the village.

qa.q: What might Ayesha have been feeling when she stopped mid-word?
qa.a: She might have been embarrassed or hurt by the remark about the ring. She later called it a sore subject.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that helped?
qa.a: She apologised gently, offered to walk with her and left the door open to talk later. That gave Ayesha space.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Ayesha's silence at first?
qa.a: She isn't sure what it means, so she guesses hurt, embarrassment or thinking, and doesn't push. Silence is ambiguous.

grounding: A teenager stops abruptly mid-sentence, which may mean hurt, embarrassment or thinking, and a friend gives space.

passage: On the team bus in Cairo, Omar sang along at the top of his voice to the song everyone knew, and the whole back row joined him, thumping the seats. He felt like part of something bigger. Later, in the empty locker room, Ivan heard him crooning a slow, old song to himself, his voice low and soft. Ivan thought it sounded sad. But when he asked, Omar shrugged and smiled. "It's my grandfather's favourite. It makes me feel proud, not sad." Ivan nodded. Songs don't always tell you what the singer feels, he thought, and he hummed along.

qa.q: Where did Omar sing along at the top of his voice?
qa.a: He sang on the team bus in Cairo.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling when he crooned the slow song in the locker room?
qa.a: He felt proud and connected to his grandfather, not sad. Ivan first thought it sounded sad, but Omar said otherwise.

qa.q: What could Ivan do when a friend's song seems to show a mood?
qa.a: Ask kindly, as he did, instead of assuming. Song choice may mirror mood, but it isn't proof.

qa.q: How might the back row have felt singing with Omar on the bus?
qa.a: They probably felt they belonged together, thumping the seats in time. Group singing can express shared identity.

grounding: A teenager sings with a group for belonging and croons privately, and lyrics do not prove what he feels.

passage: At choir practice in the school hall, Disha stepped forward for her solo verse. The song was about missing home. Her voice was clear and warm, and the hall went still. Mehak, standing in the alto row, wondered if Disha was homesick. Disha had moved to the city only last term. At the break, Mehak asked softly, "That song, is it about how you feel?" Disha laughed. "No! I just love the tune, and I wanted to be in the choir. I feel proud when I sing it. Maybe a bit homesick too, sometimes." Mehak smiled. "Both, then."

qa.q: What was Disha's solo verse about?
qa.a: It was about missing home.

qa.q: What might Disha be feeling when she sings this song?
qa.a: She feels proud and enjoys the tune, and maybe a little homesick too. She says the lyrics are not the whole story.

qa.q: What could Mehak do besides guessing from the lyrics?
qa.a: Ask gently, as Mehak did, and accept a mixed answer. Lyrics don't prove what someone feels.

qa.q: How might joining the choir help Disha?
qa.a: It gives her a group to belong to and a way to express feelings. She moved only last term.

grounding: A teenager sings a favourite song for pride and belonging, and lyrics mirror mood but do not prove it.

passage: Before my board exam I have a little ritual, Tanvir, and it's silly but true. I'm Sudha, and I put my headphones on and hum my favourite lullaby tune, quietly, in the corridor. My hands stop shaking. Last month I had a fight with my brother, the kind where doors slam. I sat on the steps humming for ten minutes, and the burn in my chest went down enough that I could talk. Humming isn't magic. I still told my mother afterwards, and that helped more. But the humming gets me to the point where I can.

qa.q: Where does Sudha hum before the exam?
qa.a: Sudha hums quietly in the corridor.

qa.q: What is Sudha feeling before exams, and what does humming do?
qa.a: Sudha is nervous, with shaking hands, and humming calms enough to steady them. It also lowers the burn in the chest after a fight.

qa.q: What could Sudha do besides humming after a fight?
qa.a: Sudha can talk to a trusted person, as Sudha told the mother. Humming gets calm enough to do so.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Sudha's humming?
qa.a: Tanvir hears it as a small ritual that helps Sudha cope. Sudha shares it as silly but true.

grounding: A teenager hums under headphones to calm nerves before an exam and after a fight, alongside talking to a trusted person.

passage: After Ms. Rao scolded the class, Leela pulled out her headphones and hummed under her breath at her desk. I'm Chetan and I sit next to her. Her face was tight at first, her fingers tapping. Slowly her jaw loosened. I couldn't tell what she was thinking. At the break I asked if she was okay, and she said, "I needed to reset. I was angry and didn't want to snap at anyone." Later that day I saw her talking to the counsellor in the corridor, so I guess the humming was step one. She looked calmer.

qa.q: What did Leela pull out after the scolding?
qa.a: She pulled out her headphones.

qa.q: What was Leela probably feeling when she hummed with a tight face?
qa.a: She was angry and trying not to snap at anyone. She said she needed to reset.

qa.q: What could Leela do alongside humming?
qa.a: Talk to a trusted person, like the counsellor, as she did later. Humming calms her, and talking helps more.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Leela's humming?
qa.a: Chetan isn't sure what she was thinking but later sees it as a first step, then sees her talk to the counsellor. Chetan notices her calmer face.

grounding: A teenager hums under headphones to calm anger after a scolding, then talks with a trusted person.

passage: Exam morning, ten minutes to the bell, and Kunal's phone buzzed. Samir, who always wrote "oi legend 😄" with three stickers, had written just "hi." No emoji. Kunal's heart dropped. Did I do something? His friend's greeting had changed. But then he remembered that Samir's paper was at nine and that Samir hated messages when he was nervous. He wrote back, "Good luck today. Coffee after?" Samir replied at noon with a row of stickers: "Legend! Yes! Sorry, brain was in physics mode." Kunal grinned. One short hello didn't mean anything.

qa.q: What did Samir usually write to Kunal?
qa.a: He usually wrote "oi legend" with three stickers.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he saw just "hi"?
qa.a: He felt a moment of worry that he'd done something to upset Samir. He stopped himself and remembered the exam.

qa.q: What could Kunal do when a greeting changes?
qa.a: Consider the context first, such as the exam, and check kindly instead of concluding. One missed reply or short hello is not proof.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when he wrote just "hi"?
qa.a: He was nervous and in physics mode, not upset with Kunal. He apologised once the exam was over.

grounding: A teenager's friend changes the greeting style, but reading too much into one short hello is a pitfall.

passage: Usha used to greet Vishal with "Vishu!!" and a shower of stickers. For two weeks now, she'd only nodded in the corridor. Vishal noticed. He wondered whether their friendship was cooling. He watched her laugh with others as usual, which confused him more. On Friday he said, "You've stopped sending stickers. Did I say something?" Usha looked surprised. "Oh! No. I got a new phone and lost all my sticker packs. And I've been in a hurry." She showed him. "I'll download them again tonight. Vishu!!" He laughed with relief.

qa.q: What did Usha use to greet Vishal with?
qa.a: She used to greet him with "Vishu!!" and a shower of stickers.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when Usha only nodded?
qa.a: He was unsure and a little worried the friendship was cooling. Her laughing with others confused him.

qa.q: What worked when Vishal asked her?
qa.a: He asked directly and kindly whether he'd said something. Her honest answer removed the worry.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Vishal asked?
qa.a: She was surprised because she hadn't realised the change mattered. She quickly offered to bring the greeting back.

grounding: A teenager's friend changes the greeting style, which may signal distance or nothing, and asking clears it.

passage: So in the debate about school plastic, I didn't just say "plastic is bad". I'm Keerthana, and I told the class to imagine their water bottles lined up from here to the gate, every single day. I drew a little diagram of a bottle's journey on the board. People sat up. Later, Sahil, you asked, "Where did you get the fact about the gate?" and I realised I'd picked the most dramatic example and hadn't checked the source properly. I went home, looked it up and corrected it next day. Good examples persuade, but they have to be true.

qa.q: What did Keerthana draw on the board?
qa.a: Keerthana drew a little diagram of a bottle's journey.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Sahil asked about the source?
qa.a: Keerthana was uneasy and realised the most dramatic example had been picked without checking. Keerthana then corrected it.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do the next time an example is used?
qa.a: Check the source before using it and pick examples that are fair, not just dramatic. Vivid examples help only if they're accurate.

qa.q: How might Sahil have seen Keerthana's debate?
qa.a: Sahil found it persuasive but asked about the source, which shows a care for accuracy. That question led Keerthana to fix it.

grounding: A teenager uses examples and a diagram to persuade peers, and learns to check sources so they are not cherry-picked.

passage: Zainab stood in front of the class to argue for earlier bedtimes. She didn't quote a rule. She said, "Your phone at ten per cent is like you at midnight, slow and grumpy." The class laughed. She drew a battery diagram on the board, and half of them nodded. I'm Rehana and I noticed she'd only picked examples that supported her. At the break I asked, "What about people who work better late?" Zainab thought, then said, "Fair. I should check that." She said she'd look for a source and add the other side in her next talk.

qa.q: What did Zainab draw on the board?
qa.a: She drew a battery diagram.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when Rehana asked about people who work better late?
qa.a: She was thoughtful and open, since she said fair and promised to check. It shows she wanted her point to be honest.

qa.q: What could Zainab do to make her argument stronger?
qa.a: Look for a source and include the other side too. Vivid examples help but can be cherry-picked.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Zainab's talk?
qa.a: Rehana finds it vivid and effective but notices the examples were one-sided, and asks kindly.

grounding: A teenager uses an analogy and diagram to persuade, and an observer notes examples can be cherry-picked, so checking matters.

passage: In the lunch queue, Deepak saw two older boys take a Class Six child's money and threaten him if he told. Deepak's stomach twisted. He had fought with one of them last year, and he knew people would say he was just getting revenge. Mahima whispered, "Are you going to tell? They'll say you're a snitch." "I'm going to tell," said Deepak. "The little one is scared." He went to the class teacher. The teacher listened without interrupting and said, "Thank you for telling me. I won't assume anything. I'll deal with this today." Deepak's shoulders relaxed and Mahima squeezed his arm.

qa.q: What did the older boys take from the Class Six child?
qa.a: They took the child's money.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he decided to tell the teacher?
qa.a: He was worried about being called a snitch, and uneasy about the younger child. He chose safety over what people might say.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond well?
qa.a: They listened, thanked him, did not assume his motives and promised to act that day. Adults should act on safety concerns.

qa.q: How might the Class Six child feel about Deepak telling?
qa.a: He was probably scared and may feel relieved that someone spoke up. Deepak acted for his safety.

grounding: A teenager reports something to an adult for safety, and the adult thanks him and listens without assuming motives.

passage:
"I read the group chat, Amma," said Charu. "They're posting nasty things about Gauri. I told the counsellor."
"Was that about a fight you had with them?" asked Lavanya.
"No. I felt sick reading it. I wasn't even angry. I just thought she shouldn't see it alone."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm proud you did."
"Some kids will say I'm a snitch."
"Maybe. But you did it for her safety, not to get them into trouble."
Charu breathed out. "The counsellor said she'd handle it carefully and not say who told."
"Good. Now come and eat."

qa.q: Who did Charu tell about the group chat?
qa.a: Charu told the counsellor.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when reading the group chat?
qa.a: Charu felt sick and worried for Gauri, not angry, and wanted Gauri not to face it alone.

qa.q: What could Charu do if other kids call Charu a snitch?
qa.a: Charu can remember acting for someone's safety and talk with the counsellor or Amma again. Adults can help keep Charu's name private.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Charu's reporting?
qa.a: She asks about motive gently, thanks Charu and says she's proud. She takes it as caring, not revenge.

grounding: A teenager reports hurtful messages out of concern for a classmate's safety, and a parent listens without assuming revenge.

passage: The canteen was loud, the bell was in five minutes, and Sachin was in a rush. "So you're saying you don't want to be group leader? Why not? What's the reason?" he fired at Chandrika. She stiffened and looked at her tray. "I never said that." Sachin realised his voice was sharp. He put his fork down. "Sorry. That sounded like an interrogation. I really want to understand. Do you want to talk at break, when it's quieter?" Chandrika's shoulders lowered. "Yes. I'm not sure myself yet." "Take your time," said Sachin. "I'll wait."

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the bell?
qa.a: The bell was in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when Sachin fired his questions?
qa.a: She felt pressured and defensive, since she stiffened and looked at her tray. She also said she wasn't sure herself.

qa.q: What could Sachin do differently next time?
qa.a: He can slow down, use a warmer tone and pick a quieter moment. Probing questions can feel like interrogation when rushed.

qa.q: How might Sachin have seen his own questions?
qa.a: He wanted to understand, but noticed his voice was sharp. He apologised and offered a quieter time.

grounding: A teenager asks confirming and probing questions that feel like interrogation, and softens his tone.

passage: After Imran missed the match, Parveen sat next to him on the wall. "So you're saying you're fine with sitting out? What's behind that?" she asked, warmly, her head tilted. Imran picked at his laces. "My knee felt off. And I didn't want to say." It felt good to be asked. The next day, a senior stopped him in the corridor and said the same thing in a hard voice: "So you're saying you're fine with sitting out? Reason?" Imran felt himself go tense and defensive. The words were nearly the same, but they landed differently.

qa.q: Where did Parveen sit next to Imran?
qa.a: She sat next to him on the wall.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when the senior asked him the same question?
qa.a: He felt tense and defensive, since the hard voice made it feel like an interrogation. With Parveen's warmth he felt supported.

qa.q: What could the senior do to make his question feel supportive?
qa.a: Use a warmer tone and show he's on Imran's side. Probing questions depend on tone and relationship.

qa.q: How might Parveen see her questions compared to the senior's?
qa.a: Parveen asked warmly as a friend and it helped him open up. The same words in a hard voice from someone less close can feel like pressure.

grounding: A teenager's confirming and probing questions feel supportive from a friend and like interrogation from a harder voice.
